Atomic persistence of sleep145-words.json and the mid-sleep kill safety (104 Z4).
Fixed, size-based sleep trigger (SLEEP_THRESHOLD): sleep is never the model's choice, which fits the automatic + mathematical rule.
Keeping rank-4/CardFold weight-update sleep as toy-only until the length wall is solved.
open_questions_for_ben: Do you want sleep to learn new relation words from examples you teach (e.g. 'Pim's nana is Ada' for 10-20 people)? This is the proposed fix to the circular labels, and it means sleep learns meanings, not facts.
Is it OK to say in the demo that sleep learns 'what a word means' rather than 'remembers facts in its weights'? Facts-in-weights is not shown live.
Should sleep run while the chat is idle (reply first, sleep afterwards), even if that means a short 'sleeping' notice in the chat?

part: Ears: the learned English reader (119 line: SciBERT plus the FrameEars / RelCondEars head)
summary: The ears are a borrowed SciBERT encoder with our frame head. The model has plenty of capacity: it reads its own training shapes perfectly (40/40 in 119f and 119g). The 119g relation-conditioned pointers were a real gain, reading 3.4 to 4.3 times as many correct facts from real sentences (91/82/100 against 24/19/27). The real bottleneck is not model size. It is how the labels and the confidence gate are built. The relation head is a single-choice (softmax) head, trained with one row per fact. Nearly half of the WebRED rows are pair-level "negatives" that get relabelled as "this sentence states no fact". The write gate is set by the single most confident wrong answer on the calibration set. Together these keep gated writes at zero by construction, even when the reading is right: on the chat-style calibration set 4,214 of 5,000 were read correctly but only 86 were written. There is also a safety bug to fix before any wiring: when the reader turns a frame into a notebook item, it invents relation names that the validator accepts. The scorer never checks these items, so M4 cannot catch it. The ears are not used by the conversation loop today (config ears47_ckpt = null). They should go in first as a shadow and then as an "ask Ben to confirm" fallback, never as a silent writer.

findings.title: Single-choice relation head plus the min-confidence gate means multi-fact sentences can never be written, and 119h makes this worse by design
findings.problem: The relation head is a softmax over 517 classes trained with cross-entropy, so it must share out 100% of its probability across relations. The gate's confidence is the minimum over act, relation, span, direction and flag probabilities, and it includes the relation's own probability. When a sentence states 2 to 4 facts and each fact is a separate row with the same text, the best the model can do is split the probability, about 1/2 to 1/4 per relation. So every frame from such a sentence has confidence of 0.5 or less, far below the gate (tau_exec 0.87 to 0.92). 119h deliberately labels every fact on the same text (5,000 rows from 1,760 sentences, about 2.8 labels per sentence), so its multi-fact frames cannot pass the gate. Also, on sentences with 4 or 5 facts (a date-range bracket plus nationality plus job, or a birthplace), probability split evenly means K=3 can drop occupation from the read-outs.
findings.evidence: scripts/fable_ears47_model.py:40 (nn.Linear(HID, n_rel)), :69 (cross_entropy on rel); scripts/fable_ears119g_score.py decode_forced_rel: mins=[p_act, p_rel, ...], conf=min(mins); taus119g.json tau_exec_single 0.870/0.887/0.918; report119g_94b_K3.json W2_writes 0/0/0 all seeds. WebRED train aggregate (data/open/webred/frames/train.jsonl): 22,069 distinct positive sentences, and 7,279 (33%) carry 2 or more relations. 119h smoke.json: rows_per_relation occ 1760 / cit 1506 / dob 1036 / dod 507 / pob 191 over 1,760 sentences.
findings.improvement: Replace the softmax relation head with a multi-label head: one yes/no (sigmoid) output per relation, trained with binary cross-entropy. Merge the rows that share a text into one training row whose target is the full set of stated relations. Decoding becomes 'every relation with p >= FLOOR, up to K' and the gate uses each relation's own probability. This is the natural next step after the 119g relation-conditioned pointers.
findings.expected_gain: Each stated relation can reach high confidence on its own, so the gate can pass true multi-fact readings. Occupation also stops competing with dates and nationality for probability. This is the precondition for any reading ever reaching the notebook.
findings.risk: Calibration changes: the temperature fit and the 47 tau rule assume one softmax, so a per-relation temperature or a shared one needs a sealed rule. Must stay one change (head plus merged targets counts as one 'label format' change and should be declared that way).

findings.title: The gate threshold is hostage to the single worst calibration error and blocks about 98% of correct readings
findings.problem: tau0 is the confidence of the single most confident wrong write on 5,000 calibration rows. tau_exec then moves it halfway to 1.0. One mislabelled row decides the whole gate, and this has already happened once: 119b/119e found a label-name mismatch that pushed tau to 0.98. On the chat-style panels the ensemble reads 4,214/5,000 calibration rows correctly but executes only 86, 43 on t_seen and 34 on t_new. gate47 and W1 fail with 0 executed. The project already has a better tool: Learn-then-Test (LTT) risk-control scripts used for abstention, and the loop config even points at abstain76 ltt_summary.json.
findings.evidence: scripts/fable_ears47_score.py:458-477 tau0_from_cal (worst=max conf of any wrong EXECUTE); fable_ears119_score.py:99,103 tau_exec=1-(1-tau0)/2 (per 119e RESULTS §2); report47g.json ens_correct cal 4214 vs ens_executed cal 86, t_seen 43, t_new 34, W1 executed 0; scripts/fable_abstain64_ltt.py and fable_abstain76_ltt.py exist; loop138i-config.json tau_hat_path -> fable-abstain76 ltt_summary.json.
findings.improvement: Replace the worst-case tau rule with an LTT (or binomial upper-bound) rule: pick the smallest tau such that the 95% upper bound on the wrong-write rate over calibration is at most a target, for example 2%. This changes scoring only, on frozen checkpoints (119g now, or 119h), so it needs no training. Seal the target rate before scoring.
findings.expected_gain: A direct measurement of how many correct writes the current readers could make at a certified wrong rate. It is likely 10 to 50 times more writes on chat-style sentences than today (SUSPECTED size), and the gate becomes robust to one bad label.
findings.risk: It certifies a small but non-zero wrong rate instead of 'zero seen on CAL'. Ben must accept that trade (the two-site rule and echo-confirm limit the harm). It must not be tuned on reading panels.

findings.title: WebRED pair-level negatives are trained as 'this sentence states no fact' and contradict positive rows for the same text
findings.problem: In WebRED, a negative means 'this particular subject-object pair does not express this relation'. It is not a statement about the whole sentence. gold_from_webred turns every negative into act NO_FACT with relation UNSURE for the whole sentence. So the same text is trained as both STATE and NO_FACT, and real fact sentences are taught to abstain. This matches doc 107's finding that 'unsure' leaks as the top relation in STATE frames (93/103/103).
findings.evidence: scripts/fable_ears47_data.py:172-176 (not positive -> NO_FACT/UNSURE) and :337-341 (all train rows enter the pool). Aggregates on data/open/webred/frames/train.jsonl: 81,517 rows, 37,437 negative (46%); 16,621 negative rows share their text with a positive row (7,284 texts). design/v3/30-modes/107 §2: 'unsure' proposed 93/103/103 times.
findings.improvement: A data-only single change: drop negative rows whose text also has a positive row, and keep NO_FACT only for texts with no positive pair at all. A stricter version keeps only negatives with unanimous votes. The step count changes, so declare it and re-assert the new count.
findings.expected_gain: Removes contradictory targets from about 20% of the pool. It should raise relation recall on real sentences and shrink the 'unsure' leak. This is the cheapest label-noise fix and tells us how much of the problem is label noise.
findings.risk: Fewer NO_FACT examples could raise invented readings on sentences with no facts. Watch the precision mark (M3) and NEG.

findings.title: The frame-to-notebook item step writes invented relation names, and the validator accepts them (safety bug before wiring)
findings.problem: When a frame is turned into a notebook item, pick_surface falls back to 'any content word in the sentence' and canonical_relation turns that word into a relation name. The unchanged listening validator then accepts the item. So a reading that is right in frame terms is written under a garbage or wrong relation. Date of birth was even written as 'birthplace', which is a wrong fact. The scorer checks the frame's class name against the gold (R106.r2_triple_of), never the rendered item, so M4 (wrong-write rate) cannot see this. Also, WebRED has 517 classes while the notebook knows 12 relations.
findings.evidence: Probe (scratch wf-ears/probe_validator.py, fictional names): 'Aldric Venmore is a Norvish pianist.' occupation -> surface 'Norvish', path ['norvish'], validator OK; "Aldric Venmore's job is pianist." occupation -> path ['venmore_s'] OK; '(born 4 March 1901) is a Norvish pianist.' date of birth -> path ['birthplace'] OK; country of citizenship -> ['norvish'] OK; 'Brisa Holloway lives in Tellimar.' residence -> ['city'] OK. LE.KNOWN_RELATIONS has 12 entries; D.N_REL = 517. Scorer: fable_ears119g_score.py score_panel_multi uses R106.r2_triple_of(fr) for W2. Code: fable_ears47_score.py:179-218 pick_surface fallback step (3).
findings.improvement: Add an explicit, sealed mapping table from ears classes to notebook relations (for example occupation->job-like relation, place of birth->birthplace, date of birth->a date-of-birth relation). Any class not in the table can only ECHO or be held in quarantine, never written. Remove the 'any content word' fallback for writes. Add a scorer mark that checks the rendered notebook item, not just the frame.
findings.expected_gain: Stops silent wrong-relation installs the moment ears start writing. Makes M4 measure what actually reaches the notebook.
findings.risk: Low. It may reduce writes for relations the notebook cannot store yet, and that is correct behaviour.

findings.title: Occupation is learned almost entirely from synthetic templates: real data has only 9 examples
findings.problem: WebRED train has 9 positive occupation examples out of 44,080 positives. Its 344 relations are dominated by 'country' (16,480) and located-in (8,531). So whatever surface cues the synthetic rows carry become the model's whole idea of occupation. 119f and 119g failed on this ('was' as the cue), and 119h tries to fix it with a richer hand template. 119g also showed a second bottleneck: even when told the relation is occupation, it read exactly only 7/2/10 of 51 occupation sentences. So 119h's M1 (at least 10/94 on 3/3 seeds) needs both better relation ranking and better spans. The 119h generator also cuts occupation labels from 5,000 to 1,760.
findings.evidence: WebRED train aggregate: occupation positives = 9; top relations country 16,480 / located-in 8,531 / contains 4,488 / citizenship 1,936. artifacts/fable-ears119g-20260922/DIRECTOR-outcome.md diagnosis 3 (oracle-relation exact 7/2/10 of 51). 119h smoke.json occupation rows 1,760.
findings.improvement: Read the 119h outcome this way. PASS: occupation now rises through relation ranking and span learning, so next run the LTT gate scoring (finding 2) on the frozen 119h checkpoints, then the multi-label head. FAIL with occupation ranked high but spans wrong: the templates are still too narrow, so the next single change is more realistic sentence shapes, ideally Qwen-written varied biography sentences (Ben allowed Qwen practice sentences) with fictional names. FAIL with occupation still ranked low: this is softmax probability splitting, so the next change is the multi-label head (finding 1). FAIL with precision collapsing: remove the contradictory negatives (finding 3).
findings.expected_gain: Each outcome maps to one pre-decided next change, so no 119i guesswork is needed.
findings.risk: The decision rule needs the descriptive numbers 119h already reports (occupation rank, training-shape check, oracle-relation read). If any are missing, add them to the post-run diagnosis, never to the marks.

findings.title: Wire the ears into the loop as shadow first, then as an 'ask Ben to confirm' fallback, never as a silent writer
findings.problem: Today the loop hears only through the rule chain (bench73 + fake). The learned ears are not wired in (ears47_ckpt null). They are also nowhere near a silent-write gate, even on chat-style sentences (86/5,000 executed). The reading job (encyclopedia prose, 517 WebRED classes) and the chat job (Ben's sentences, 12 notebook relations) are different tasks being scored on one head.
findings.evidence: artifacts/fable-agent138i-20260922/loop138i-config.json ears.chain ['bench73','fake'], ears47_ckpt null; report47g.json gate47_reported false, W1 executed 0; TAU_ECHO = 0.5 (fable_ears47_score.py:36) means ECHO is available at much lower confidence.
findings.improvement: Step 1 (S): shadow mode. Run the ears in parallel with the rule chain on every turn and log agreement and disagreement. It never writes. Step 2 (M, after finding 4 is fixed): only when the rule chain says 'didn't understand', turn an ears frame with confidence at or above TAU_ECHO into a confirm question through the existing yes/no tick ('Did you mean: Aldric Venmore's job is pianist?'). Ben's yes is the write, marked as taught by Ben. For web reading, keep the frames in the thinker's quarantine and let the two-site rule do the promoting. Inference is one sentence at a time on the Mac CPU with one copied checkpoint.
findings.expected_gain: The rule loop can handle phrasings it does not cover yet, with no new safety risk (a human confirms every write). The shadow logs give real chat data about where the ears help, which is useful for the demo ('it learned to understand my odd phrasing').
findings.risk: Too many confirm questions would annoy Ben. Cap it at one per turn and only on rule-chain misses. Needs the relation map (finding 4) first, or confirmations will show nonsense relation names.

findings.title: A cheaper design: shrink the relation vocabulary to what the notebook can store, plus OTHER
findings.problem: The head spends its capacity on 517 WebRED classes, but only 12 notebook relations (plus a few reading relations such as occupation and birth/death dates) can ever be used. The large inventory is where 'country' vs 'located-in' vs 'citizenship' confusion and namespace remaps (119b/119e) come from.
findings.evidence: D.N_REL = 517 vs LE.KNOWN_RELATIONS = 12 (probe p2.py); 119b remap and 119e label-namespace diagnosis; doc 107 §2 (errors are namespace-shaped).
findings.improvement: Train the head on about 20 useful relations plus one OTHER class (collapse the rest), keeping the pointers. Cheaper still for web reading: a plain-software placeholder for the 4 or 5 relations in the first sentence of a Wikipedia article, scored on the same panel as the learned ears, with the two-site rule as the gate.
findings.expected_gain: Fewer confusable classes, a relation map that is trivially complete, and faster calibration. Gives a baseline that shows how much the learned ears really add.
findings.risk: Loses long-tail relations that the benchmark goal (MQuAKE-style) might want later. The placeholder must be labelled as plain software in any claim.

findings.title: Add a cheap label-structure audit before each ears GPU wave
findings.problem: 119b, 119e, 119f and 119g each failed on a data or label assumption that simple counts would have shown: name mismatch, one fact per sentence, template cues. The counts in this review (9 occupation positives, 33% multi-fact texts, 16,621 contradictory negatives) take seconds on the Mac and use training data only.
findings.evidence: This review's aggregates on train.jsonl (under 10 s, no panel opened); 119e RESULTS §2 (346 old-name golds found only after a failed wave); 119f/119g DIRECTOR diagnoses.
findings.improvement: A sealed audit script prints, per pool: rows per relation (real vs synthetic), texts with conflicting targets, relations per text, the share of negatives, and the target relation's real-data count. The director reads it before approving a wave.
findings.expected_gain: Catches predictable failures before 40 minutes of GPU time, so fewer registered FAILs.
findings.risk: Very low. It reads training pools only and never panels.

keep_as_is: Relation-conditioned pointers (119g). They delivered 3.4 to 4.3 times more exact readings at about 2 times the precision, so keep them under any head change.
The one-change, sealed, per-seed discipline and always reporting K=1 alongside K=3. It made each failure's cause diagnosable.
The director's frozen-checkpoint diagnosis habit, including fresh fictional sentences kept outside the repo. It found the 'was' cue and the one-slot limit.
Keeping reading panels sealed and scorer-only, and never tuning K, FLOOR or tau on them.
A borrowed SciBERT encoder for now (per Ben's ruling). Capacity is not the bottleneck: training shapes are read 40/40.
The never-write-unless-sure principle and the ECHO path. The fix is to make the gate measurable (LTT), not to drop it.
Web text stays quarantined, with the two-site rule as the promotion gate for anything the ears read online.
open_questions_for_ben: What are the learned ears for in the next month: understanding your chat sentences (the demo) or reading web or encyclopedia text (the benchmark)? The answer decides whether the next change targets the 12 notebook relations or the WebRED inventory.

Is it OK for the loop to ask 'Did you mean ...? (yes/no)' when the rule-based ears don't understand you, with your yes counting as the teach? That is the safe way to use the learned ears before they can write alone.

Will you accept a gate that certifies a small wrong-write rate (for example at most 2%, with a 95% confidence bound) instead of 'zero wrong seen on calibration'? Today's rule blocks about 98% of correct readings.

part: Notebook memory, the daemon, and robustness (memory-daemon)
summary: The notebook itself is solid. It is an append-only, hash-chained log that is fsynced and read back before the agent says "Saved". It repairs a torn last line on boot, refuses to start if a line in the middle is corrupted, never lets inferences or sleep rows stand beside a taught row, and keeps the old values in the log. Speed is not a problem at demo size. My probe taught 400 facts in 2 ms per turn, answered questions in 2 ms (5 ms worst), and rebooted with 800 events in 0.01 s (the 170 index is working). I found the root cause of the "mailbox race". It is not a bug in the current base. It keeps showing up because most single-fix experiments sit on daemon classes that inherit the old exp-74 run loop, which has no 141 settle gate, and the test harnesses write inbox files non-atomically. The weak spots are in what the store records, not in how durably it records it. Events have no timestamp, no original sentence and no speaker, so "when/who told you?" cannot be answered. Some display state is lost on restart. A correction-shaped sentence ("used to be X but now it is Y") gets stored as a nonsense relation.

findings.title: Mailbox race root cause: single-fix loops run the pre-141 daemon loop
findings.problem: Registered G2 FAILs keep being blamed on 'the mailbox race' (153, 155, 158, 166, 192...). The 141 settle gate only reaches the 138b/138i merge lineage. Every single-piece loop built on the loop150/162b lineage still runs D74.Daemon.run, which serves any *.txt the moment it appears. The sealed harnesses (fable_redteam110_runner.Driver.send line 178, the marks123 soak send, fable_marks123_all.py lines 159/243/793) write with plain write_text (create the file, then write the bytes). A poll that lands between those two steps serves an empty message and replies 'I didn't catch anything.'
findings.evidence: Probe (MRO introspection): Loop138iDaemon.run and Loop193Daemon.run come from fable_loop138b_agent (settle-gated, lines ~405-410). Loop192, Loop173b, Loop166, Loop158, Loop155, Loop153 and Loop138c .run all come from fable_daemon74_run (no gate). The marks138g/138h/138i soaks are each 2000 turns, 0 lost, 0 wrong. 115 post-141 rt110 reports contain non-D-case 'catch anything' replies only in runs of ungated loops (e.g. marks155 T2/T3/T5/D3, marks166 R5 msg_02, marks138c P4/U1, marks153 P4). The 192 RESULTS blames a 'startup mailbox race' on loop192, which is also ungated.
findings.improvement: Smallest fix, harness side: at runtime, patch the marks123 runner so every inbox write is atomic (write '.<name>.tmp', then os.replace to '<name>.txt'). This is the same runtime-patch pattern marks123 already uses for R110.daemon_cmd, so no sealed file is edited. It protects every daemon, gated or not. Also rule that new single fixes subclass the 138i daemon (settle + 108), not loop150-era bases.
findings.expected_gain: The flaky registered G2 FAILs and the open re-runs they force go away. Suite comparisons measure the change again instead of machine load. This likely saves 5-15 minutes and one ambiguous verdict per experiment.
findings.risk: The harness patch changes the timing of the harness, not what it judges. It should be pre-registered once as a harness change, with before/after verdict equality on one clean base (138i) to show nothing moved.

findings.title: Frozen reference runs contain race artefacts, so later diffs move for no reason
findings.problem: Some registered base runs recorded an empty-serve line as if it were the truth. Every later run on the same suite then shows a 'move' there, which agents have to explain away as 'log-only race'.
findings.evidence: artifacts/fable-me166-20260922/marks166/rt110-report.json R5 msg_02 = 'I didn't catch anything.' (a race). artifacts/fable-me166c-20260922/RESULTS.md: both the registered run and the open re-run 'moved' that same line to 'I already have that.', the correct reply. The 173/173b board entries show the same 'rt110 log-only race on both runs' pattern.
findings.improvement: After the atomic-writer patch, regenerate one clean reference marks run for the current base (138i) and point all future G2 comparisons at it. In the diff tool, flag any reference line equal to 'I didn't catch anything.' on a non-empty message as REFERENCE-INVALID instead of counting it as a move.
findings.expected_gain: Removes a standing false 'move' from every comparison, so nobody has to explain it again or re-run.
findings.risk: Low. It needs one registered re-baseline run (about 3 min of Mac CPU).

findings.title: The notebook forgets when, who and what was actually said
findings.problem: FACT events store actor/source and a normalized 'raw' string such as 'teach Tovi city = Brell'. They store no wall-clock time, no original English sentence and no speaker. The per-fact origin (self_origin) and the turn log live only in memory. So 'Who told you that?', 'When did I tell you?' and 'How do you know X?' all fail, even though these are exactly the 'questions about itself' the uncle/dad demo wants. It also blocks recency-aware forgetting and time-scoped facts later.
findings.evidence: Probe: last event JSON has keys actor, deps, event_id, fact_id, kind, n, prev, provenance(null), raw('correct Rukakax city = Zzorbo'), relation, rule_id, source, subject, supersedes, v, value. There is no time or sentence field. Probe replies: 'Who taught you that Tovi's city is Brell?', 'How do you know Tovi's city?' and 'What did I teach you?' each got the double refusal, before and after a reboot. fable_loop138_agent.py:232-243 keeps self_origin/self_turn_log in memory only.
findings.improvement: One additive change: the listening path puts {'t': ISO time, 'said': original sentence, 'by': 'Ben'} into the FACT event's existing 'provenance' field (it is already in the schema and null for taught rows). The self-answerer then reads origin from the notebook instead of from memory. No existing rule changes. The hash chain covers the new fields automatically.
findings.expected_gain: Enables demo lines like 'You told me that on Sept 22 at 9:14: "Tovi's city is Brell."', which a plain transformer cannot do. It survives restarts and gives the base for forgetting and 'used to be' later.
findings.risk: Changes event bytes, so frozen byte-level comparisons of events.jsonl will move (expected, predictable). It must not alter the dedupe keys (value equality), or re-teaches would stop deduping.

findings.title: 'X's city used to be A but now it is B' writes a junk relation
findings.problem: A natural correction sentence is saved as a brand-new functional relation named 'city_used_to_be_brell_but_now_it' with value Varn. The real city stays Brell, and the reply echoes the junk back as 'Saved'. This is a wrong write that the relation-name path lets through because any 'X's <words> is Y' becomes a relation.
findings.evidence: Probe dialog 03: 'Tovi's city is Brell.' then 'Tovi's city used to be Brell but now it is Varn.' -> 'Saved: Tovi's city used to be brell but now it is Varn.' events.jsonl: RELATION 'city_used_to_be_brell_but_now_it' functional=True; FACT value Varn. 'What is Tovi's city?' -> 'Tovi's city is Brell.' Open-vocabulary relations also accept 'second city' and 'favourite thing in the whole world' (these may be fine).
findings.improvement: Add a store-side relation-name screen: refuse (clarify) any new relation name that contains a copula or tense word ('is', 'was', 'used to be', 'but', 'now', 'no longer'), or that is longer than about 4 words. Better still, route 'used to be A but now B' to the correction path. This is one guard at the point where RELATION events get declared.
findings.expected_gain: Closes a class of wrong writes that is easy to trigger in a live demo. Keeps the notebook's relation list clean as it grows.
findings.risk: It could refuse some legitimate long relation names. Measure it against the 600-row bench and the session suites (expect 0 moves).

findings.title: Display-case fix (166c) is lost on restart
findings.problem: The capital letter learned from the first Title-case mention is kept only in memory (loop._dc166c), so answers change after a reboot. A demo that restarts the daemon (or crashes) will show the inconsistency.
findings.evidence: Probe: 'pip's city is Varn.', 'Pip is nice.', 'What is pip's city?' -> "Pip's city is Varn." After rebuilding the daemon on the same directory: -> "pip's city is Varn." fable_loop138i_agent.py sets loop._dc166c = {}; fable_loop166c_agent.py:114-117,183 has no persistence.
findings.improvement: Rebuild _dc166c on boot by replaying the display rule over the notebook's ENTITY/ALIAS events and the turn log. Or record a small DISPLAY event (append-only, it does not touch facts).
findings.expected_gain: Answers look the same before and after a restart.
findings.risk: Low. It is cosmetic, but it moves reply text in suites that restart mid-case (p2 restart cases).

findings.title: Most off-script inputs get a contradictory double refusal
findings.problem: Unhandled turns reply with two stacked fallbacks: 'I do not know that from what you taught me. I have no record of it, so I will not guess. I didn't understand that, I don't know — could you say it another way?' This says both 'I don't know' and 'I didn't understand'. It will appear whenever the uncle/dad go off-script.
findings.evidence: Probe: 'Who told you that?', 'How sure are you about Tovi's city?', "Tovi doesn't speak Ketan anymore.", 'My friend Quen says ...', 'Who lives in Ci...?' and 'Pip is nice.' all returned this exact 2-part text.
findings.improvement: When the ears produce no parse, emit only the 'didn't understand' template and suppress the notebook 'no record' template (the question never reached the notebook). This is one guard where the replies get joined.
findings.expected_gain: Every failure sounds honest and clear instead of confused, which matters most in the live demo.
findings.risk: Moves many reply texts in the suites (predictable, text only, no writes).

findings.title: Exactly-once relies on re-executing turns being harmless
findings.problem: 108's boot_reconcile re-runs a mailbox turn whose reply was not yet durable. That is safe for teaches, asks and same-value corrections, which dedupe by value. It is not proven for stateful turns: a 'yes' that answers a pending change question, a two-step clarify, or a turn that lands during sleep. Event ids include the turn counter, so dedupe rests only on value equality.
findings.evidence: design/v3/30-modes/108-daemon-exactly-once-muse.md section 2 ('Re-execution is fact-safe: teaches dedupe..., corrections supersede to the same value'). Event id format seen in probe: 'turn00402-fact-5b841e90'. 141 R4 tested 12 aimed kill-9s on teach/ask streams only.
findings.improvement: Make the event_id deterministic from the mailbox file name plus the action index (e.g. 's00123-a0'). The existing _dup(event_id) check then gives true exactly-once for every write, whatever the pending-question state. Test with kill-9 aimed at 'yes' and forget turns.
findings.expected_gain: Turns crash safety from 'probably idempotent' into a guarantee, which is a claim an expert reviewer can check.
findings.risk: Changes event ids. In-process test callers that don't use file names need a fallback id.

keep_as_is: Append-only hash-chained events.jsonl with fsync plus read-back before 'Saved' (fable_notebook_contract.py:164-178): the right durability core.
Torn-tail repair keeps the torn bytes in torn-tail.txt, and a bad middle line makes the daemon refuse to boot (loud, never silent).

current() never lets inferred or sleep rows stand beside a taught row. A conflict on a functional relation asks before changing, and old values stay in the log (probe: contradiction -> 'Do you want me to change it to Zzorbo?', 'Actually,...' supersedes, answer updates, reboot keeps it).
Forget is a RETRACT event, not a delete, and re-teaching works afterwards (probe).
Multi-valued relations work ('Tovi speaks Ketan/Morvish' -> both kept).
Per-turn cost is flat: 2 ms per teach from 50 to 400 facts, ask median 2 ms, reboot of 800 events 0.01 s (the 170 index keeps it this fast).
The 141 settle gate plus 108 reconcile in the 138b/138i daemon lineage (138g/h/i soaks: 2000 turns, 0 lost, 0 wrong).
The demo client fable_demo126_run.py already writes inbox files atomically (tmp + os.replace, lines 311-314), and the settle daemon skips dot/tmp files.
open_questions_for_ben: Should new single-fix experiments be required to build on the 138i daemon (settle + exactly-once), so the old exp-74 loop is retired from registered runs?
Is it OK to add time + original sentence + speaker to every taught fact's provenance? It is the basis for 'when/who told you' demo answers, but it changes event bytes going forward.
For open-vocabulary relations ('second city', 'favourite thing in the whole world'): do you want these saved, or should long or odd relation names get a clarify question?

summary: The safe core works well. The notebook contract, the zero-wrong-writes discipline, the demo harness (demo126 PASS) and the notebook arm on Fable-Edit-200 (100/100 two-hop, 50/50 reversal, 50/50 abstain) are all solid. But since about piece 129, most build effort has gone into hand-written English phrase rules for the conversation loop (pieces 129-193: tail words, fillers, titles, apostrophes, lowercase, small talk, say-again, and so on). Ben's final own-weights model cannot inherit these rules, and they still generalise poorly. My probe of the current base 138i understood only about 7 of 16 natural fictional turns. It also stores boss, employer and manager as three unrelated relations, so two-hop questions over naturally taught facts fail. The learned parts are pointed at the wrong targets. The ears are grinding on encyclopedia sentences (WebRED occupation 1/94), not on the chat and edit-sentence English that conversation and MQuAKE need. The benchmark result so far feeds the notebook triples, so it measures a database, not Ben's model. Also, its design is essentially the published GWalk baseline on MQuAKE-Remastered, which an expert will point out. The path converges only if the rule loop is changed from "the product" into "the teacher and safety checker" for an own-weights reader, and if the benchmark is run on the public corrected dataset with English input.

findings.title: Stop the phrase-rule treadmill; make the rule loop the teacher for an own-weights chat reader
findings.problem: Each new phrasing gets its own sealed piece (60+ pieces since 129, mostly one wording each). Every fix finds more gaps, and none of this work carries over into Ben's own-weights model. Coverage of natural English is still low.
findings.evidence: design/v3/30-modes/ piece files 129-193 (tailwords 139c/d/e, filler 157/157b/157c, title 157c, smalltalk 156/b/c, sayagain 189/189b, apos 193, lowercase 180/180b...). Board line 5 'QUEUED for after layer C' lists more phrase-list fixes (189c repeat phrasings, 'about' widening). Probe on loop138i (scratchpad wf-strategy/run1): 'My sister Oriel is a nurse.', 'Oriel moved to Brask last year.', 'Kell is in Varnia.', 'Where does Kavo's boss live?', 'Which city is Kavo's boss based in?', 'Is Dovan from Varnia?' all got the generic don't-understand reply. 'What country was Dovan born in?' got the city Kell.
findings.improvement: Freeze the rule loop at 138j for anything that is not a safety fix. Build one learned own-weights reader that maps a chat utterance to the same structured line the loop already produces. Train it on (a) every utterance-to-structured-line pair the loop and its suites have logged, and (b) many generated paraphrases (Qwen/GPT may write practice sentences, per ears-decisions), labelled by the loop where it is confident. The notebook contract plus echo-confirm stays as the safety gate, so a learned reader can never silently write a wrong fact. Score it against the rule loop on a sealed fresh-paraphrase panel. The learned reader should win on coverage while wrong writes stay at 0.
findings.expected_gain: Every later hour of work goes into Ben's own weights rather than throwaway rules. Coverage of natural phrasing should grow much faster than one phrasing per piece. This learned reader is also the part that makes the benchmark and the demo 'his model'.
findings.risk: A small from-scratch reader may be weaker than the rules at first. Keep the rules as fallback and safety net and switch per utterance by confidence. Training data written by the placeholder LLM is weaker than real user text.

findings.title: Benchmark on public MQuAKE-Remastered with English input, and compare to GWalk
findings.problem: The expert-facing result so far is Fable-Edit-200, a home-built 200-item set, and the notebook arm was fed triples, not English. The notebook design (walk a knowledge graph of edited facts) is essentially GWalk, the ICLR 2025 baseline that already beats state of the art on MQuAKE-Remastered. An expert will ask 'how is this different from GWalk, and who did the parsing?'. The comparison model, SmolLM2-360M, is not the same size and was not trained on the same data, and the RAG-lite arm scored below plain in-context (38 vs 52 of 150), which suggests it was a weak baseline.
findings.evidence: artifacts/fable-bench65-20260921/RESULTS.md ('This arm feeds TRIPLES, not English'). artifacts/fable-bench66-20260921/RESULTS.md (RAG-lite 38/150 < in-context 52/150, P66.2 FALSE). artifacts/fable-bench125-20260922 (English loop113 145/50/5 on s2fresh 4-hop). grep: no RESULTS.md mentions MQuAKE-Remastered; it appears only in plan docs 63/70/71/92. GWalk: https://github.com/henryzhongsc/MQuAKE-Remastered and https://iclr.cc/virtual/2025/poster/28478
findings.improvement: Register one run on MQuAKE-Remastered CF-3k with the standard multi-hop accuracy metric. Arms: (1) notebook fed the benchmark's English edit sentences and questions through the own-weights reader (or the rule loop, labelled as such); (2) the published GWalk and MeLLo numbers; (3) Ben's own same-size plain transformer, trained on the same text; (4) a proper retrieval baseline. Present the claim honestly: 'a tiny own-weights system matches a GWalk-style editor that normally uses a large LLM, and abstains instead of guessing'. The small size and the abstention are the parts an expert can respect.
findings.expected_gain: A result on a public, corrected, cited dataset with a known state-of-the-art line, instead of a self-built set. This is the one benchmark result an expert is likely to take seriously.
findings.risk: MQuAKE question wording is varied, and the rule parser may do poorly on it. That is informative and it motivates finding 1. Never tune on the test split; build the parser only on CF-6334 train.

findings.title: Point the ears at the English that matters now; pause the WebRED occupation grind
findings.problem: The learned ears (borrowed encoder) have spent the 119, 119b-h waves on real encyclopedia sentences. That serves web reading in THINKING mode, which is parked and lower priority. Conversation and MQuAKE need short chat and cloze-style sentences, where the ears were already fairly good but too timid.
findings.evidence: Board: 119f registered FAIL (occupation 1/94). 119g FAIL (occupation 1/94 on every seed). Morning report: real-text reading 0 saves on 3/3 seeds. artifacts/fable-ears47-20260921/RESULTS.md: on generated sentences R2-NEW 2,682/3,000 correct but only 640 executed, and 0 of 46 WebRED executed.
findings.improvement: After the 119h wave finishes, pause WebRED waves. Re-target the same ears training setup to the conversation domain plus MQuAKE edit sentences, which merges it with finding 1 (one learned reader, not two). Calibrate the execute threshold on a chat-domain panel so it stops being timid.
findings.expected_gain: The GPU goes to the reader Ben will actually talk to and to the benchmark, instead of a mode that is parked.
findings.risk: Real-web reading is delayed. That is acceptable because web text cannot go into weights without two sites anyway.

findings.title: Relations are not canonical: boss, employer and manager become three different relations
findings.problem: Facts taught in natural words go under different relation names, so a two-hop question worded differently from how the fact was taught fails. This hits the core pitch (two-hop over taught facts) in a live demo.
findings.evidence: Probe: 'Kavo works for Lirae.' -> 'Saved: Kavo's employer is Lirae.'; 'Lirae lives in Tamsin.' saved; 'Where does Kavo's boss live?' -> don't-understand; 'Kavo's manager is Lirae.' -> 'Saved: Kavo's manager is Lirae.' (a new relation, not recognised as a repeat).
findings.improvement: Add a relation-canonicalisation layer: a small fixed synonym map now, and in the learned reader, output one canonical relation ID with aliases. Echo-confirm when a new relation name looks close to an existing one.
findings.expected_gain: Two-hop questions work over facts taught in any wording. This is also needed for MQuAKE, whose relations are Wikidata IDs.
findings.risk: Over-merging near-synonyms (boss vs employer can differ). The echo-confirm prevents silent errors.

findings.title: Shortest demo path: freeze a base and compare against Ben's own same-size transformer
findings.problem: The demo needs to show an advantage over a plain transformer of equal size. The current side-by-side uses a borrowed SmolLM2-360M, a different size and different training data. Meanwhile Ben already has a from-scratch talker pretrained on 617M tokens, own weights, which is a natural 'plain transformer, same data' control.
findings.evidence: artifacts/fable-demo126-20260922/RESULTS.md (A1-A8 PASS on loop117 and loop113b, run in about 7 s). Morning report: talker pretraining done (617M tokens, BLiMP 67.4%); talker120b raw unfaithful 172/500, 0/500 after the brake.
findings.improvement: Freeze 138j (or 138i) plus the demo126 script as the demo base. Add the grounded self card. As the plain-transformer foil, use Ben's own pretrained talker with the taught sentences in its prompt, scored with the same script (teach, two-hop, correct, restart, 'I don't know'). The mouth can be the braked talker for flavour. Then stop adding features for the demo.
findings.expected_gain: A demo ready in about a day with a fair, easy-to-explain comparison: same person, same data, same size, one with the notebook architecture and one without.
findings.risk: The foil may still get a few two-hop items right in-context, which is fine and honest. Rehearse off-script questions, since the rule loop fails on many natural phrasings (finding 1).

findings.title: Garbled double refusal in replies
findings.problem: When a turn is not understood, the reply joins two templates into one confusing sentence. Uncle and dad would see this on any off-script question.
findings.evidence: Probe, many turns: "I do not know that from what you taught me. I have no record of it, so I will not guess. I didn't understand that, I don't know — could you say it another way?"
findings.improvement: Give one reply per failure status: 'I didn't understand that; could you say it another way?' vs 'I don't know that yet.'
findings.expected_gain: Clearer and more honest behaviour in the demo; it also separates 'I didn't understand' from 'I don't know' (abstention) in logs.
findings.risk: Frozen suites will show predicted reply-only moves.

findings.title: Use lighter process for plain-software reply and phrase pieces; refresh the stale Next-up list
findings.problem: Full sealing, ledgers and registered-FAIL rules on wording-level rule changes cost a lot of agent and director time (disk, database and network incidents, re-registrations such as 180 -> 180b, 187 -> 187b, 164 -> 164b). The board's 'Next up' section still lists 21-Sep items (mouth53 re-dispatch, 'first registered benchmark run from 63').
findings.evidence: Board lines 260-268 (Next up) are stale compared with the Running section. Morning report lists registered FAILs 180, 187, 170, 167c where 'the feature often works'. The outside review (design/v3/28) already accepted 'lighter manifests for cheap diagnostics'.
findings.improvement: Keep full sealing for learned-model experiments and benchmark runs. For plain-software reply and phrase fixes, use a single regression suite with a zero-wrong-writes gate. Rewrite Next-up around the three direction changes above.
findings.expected_gain: Frees director and agent capacity for the learned reader and the benchmark.
findings.risk: Some loss of rigour on rule pieces, which matters little if they are frozen anyway.

keep_as_is: Notebook contract (append-only, stable IDs, discrete statuses, taught beats inferred): it is the part that makes answers true by construction and is the natural safety gate for any learned reader.
Zero-wrong-writes safety discipline and echo-confirm on risky writes (360-turn red team 152: 0 wrong writes).
Sealed registration, pre-registered marks and 'FAIL stays FAIL' for learned-model and benchmark experiments.
demo126 harness (teach, two-hop, forget, refuse, clarify, abstain; A1-A8 PASS) as the demo backbone.
bench125-style same-metric tables with correct/abstain/wrong reported separately, never averaged.
Braked own-weights talker (0/500 wrong after the brake): a real own-architecture mouth.
Automatic router/rank-limited sleep line (exp 43E/43I/44/46): a genuine own-weights learning mechanism worth keeping as research.
open_questions_for_ben: Are you OK freezing the rule-based conversation loop (safety fixes only) and moving build effort to one learned own-weights reader that the rules help train?
For the uncle/dad demo, may the 'plain transformer' foil be your own pretrained talker, given the same taught sentences in its prompt? That is the fairest same-size, same-data comparison.
For the benchmark, are you comfortable stating plainly that the memory design resembles GWalk (ICLR 2025), with the claimed advantage being a tiny own-weights system plus honest abstention?
Can the ears GPU time move from encyclopedia reading (WebRED) to chat and MQuAKE sentences after the 119h wave?

summary: The honesty machinery works. Seals are checked, post-seal edits get caught (180, 187, 164, 167 were all turned into registered FAILs), and each accepted piece gets a held-out probe from the director. That is worth keeping. The time goes to four places. (1) Every piece writes its own comparison harness, about 700 lines for 192, and these hand-written harnesses cause many of the post-seal edits and case-file bugs. (2) The frozen suites grade reply wording as if it were correctness. marks123 shows FAIL on 5 of its 10 suites even for the accepted base, and changing only the reply text registers as "wrong". (3) Agents are built on old bases (192 on 167e, 190 on 138g) while the real base moves on, so merges pile up to 9–11 pieces. The 11-piece merge 138d failed, and wording clashes like 192 vs 154g only show up at merge time. (4) Wait time: after a network drop the agent sat idle about 45–55 minutes before relaunch, and finished reports waited another 45–55 minutes for the director to verify them. A clean small piece takes about 1 hour from brief to verified (193: 09:56 to 10:50). A piece hit by an outage takes about 3.2–3.6 hours (192, 196), and roughly half of that is waiting.

findings.title: One shared, sealed comparison tool instead of a new diff harness per piece
findings.problem: Each piece writes its own suites/marksdiff/bench drivers. They are rewritten, not copied, so each one is a fresh chance for bugs. Agents also spend much of their run reading the 1156-line marks123 source to work out why a case moved. Driver bugs found after the seal force disclosed re-runs, or turn into registered FAILs.
findings.evidence: 96 per-piece harness scripts in scripts/ (marksdiff/_suites/_bench). 192: 231 lines of feature code in fable_fix192_correctreply.py vs about 730 lines of harness (bench 132, marksdiff 204, probe 141, suites 254). 138i: m1pieces 542 + suites 557 + m2 237. The harness pairs share little code: fix167e_marksdiff vs fix192_marksdiff differ on 159 of about 220 lines; fix188_suites vs fix193_suites differ on 514 lines. Transcript 192 go1 mentions fable_marks123_all 23 times, mostly sed/grep reads of its source (lines 100-140, 460-510, 767-875). Board: post-seal driver fixes on 163, 164, 166b, 173b, 171b, 154d.
findings.improvement: Director builds and seals one tool once, e.g. scripts/fable_suitediff.py --agent X --config Y --base-rows Z. It runs redteam136, redteam143, sessions152, marks123 and the bench, and writes a per-case moves JSON (id, old verdict/reply/stored, new verdict/reply/stored, class: reply-only / stored / verdict). Briefs then say: 'predicted moves = a JSON list of ids plus class; the tool checks it.' Base rows are cached per accepted base, so a piece only runs its own side. Piece agents write only the feature code and the piece's own case file.
findings.expected_gain: Roughly 30-40% of agent time per piece, and it removes a whole class of post-seal driver fixes. The director can verify by running one command.
findings.risk: A bug in the shared tool would hit every piece. To guard against that, seal it, test it on two past pieces whose results are known (192, 190b) before adopting it, and change it only in its own registered experiment.

findings.title: Frozen suites grade reply wording as correctness; retire the stale suite-level bars
findings.problem: marks123's suite-level PASS/FAIL no longer means anything. The accepted base reads FAIL on p2, p3, p4, bench and rt81. The soak counts a correct write as 'wrong' unless the reply starts with 'Saved:'. So any reply-text change produces scary FAIL or 'wrong' numbers that every agent must explain, and that the director has to rule 'FAIL by construction'. The same kind of literal-text check also produced a registered FAIL for 137d (the judges expected the old HEARSAY_MSG).
findings.evidence: scripts/fable_marks123_all.py:854 `if not (reply.strip().startswith("Saved:") or reply.strip() == "I already have that."): wrong += 1`. artifacts/fable-agent138i-20260922/marks138i/fable_marks123_summary.json: p2 FAIL, p3 FAIL (l2/l5z1/l5z2), p4 FAIL, bench FAIL (edit_200 wrong 99, s2fresh 0 correct under the stock driver), rt81 FAIL. 138i RESULTS says 'suite bars read FAIL at suite level by construction'. 192 RESULTS: soak 'wrong 41 = 39 Actually->Updated' with the notebook audit clean; redteam143 Q1-Q7 turned into HARNESS-ERROR; rt81 5 OK->UNCLEAR; l5z1 9 SAVED->WRITE_OTHER, all caused by the wording alone. Board 07:49: 137d registered FAIL on 7 reply-text checks with 0 stores.
findings.improvement: Register 'frozen suites v2' as one director experiment. Every judge scores the stored facts and events (what the notebook actually holds), plus a separate 'reply mentions the right value' check. No literal checks on prefixes like 'Saved:'. Suite-level bars are re-set to the current base's absolute counts: wrong writes, wrong answers, lost/doubled facts. The main gate stays per-case diff vs base. Keep v1 frozen for history, but stop requiring agents to explain its suite labels.
findings.expected_gain: Removes most of the 'FAIL by construction' prose and the per-case wording triage (in 192 this took a large share of both runs). Verdicts become easier to read and harder to misread, for Ben and for the uncle demo story.
findings.risk: Re-baselining could hide a real regression if done carelessly. Do it once, sealed, on the accepted base, and have both versions report side by side for a few pieces.

findings.title: Build every piece on the current base and merge in small batches
findings.problem: Pieces are built on whatever base existed when they were briefed (192 on 167e, 190 on 138g, 164b on 138h), while the base moves 138g -> 138h -> 138i. Merges then stack 9-11 pieces, need port plans and long lists of cross-piece 'interaction classes', and reveal clashes late. For example, 192's 'Updated: ... (it was Sam).' and 154g's 'Saved: ... (It was Z.)' are two wordings for the same event, found only when planning the 138j merge. Big merges are the slowest and most failure-prone step.
findings.evidence: Board 07:42: 138d (11 pieces) registered FAIL on M4/M5/M6. 138i RESULTS M1: 173b 58/94, 167d 22/32, 171b 120/122, each diff a listed 'interaction class'. 196 brief is about 5.4 KB and needed a director resume note. Board line 9: 205 merge138j has 11 pieces with a 150 min deadline, and the director had to rule on a wording clash. 192 brief: 'ONE CHANGE on loop167e'. 190b base is loop190, which sits on 138g.
findings.improvement: Rule: a new piece always builds on the newest accepted base. Right after it is verified, a small 'land' step (1-3 pieces, run by the shared diff tool) makes it the new base. Pieces already running on old bases get merged in batches of at most 4. The one-change rule is kept: 'land' changes no behaviour, and its marks are just replay-identical to each piece.
findings.expected_gain: Removes the multi-hour layer merges and most interaction-class bookkeeping. Clashes appear within one piece instead of 10. The time saving here is estimated, not measured.
findings.risk: Pieces running in parallel against the same base can conflict with each other. Landing order must be serial, and a piece whose base went stale gets a quick re-run on the new base before landing.

findings.title: Cut the waiting time: automatic resume and a mechanical verify step
findings.problem: In the two slow pieces, agent work was about 2 hours but total time was about 3.5 hours. About 45-55 minutes went on relaunching after network or database failures, and another 45-55 minutes on reports waiting for the director to verify them one at a time. The mechanical checks (seal intact, what changed after the seal, whether RESULTS numbers match the JSON) are done by hand each time.
findings.evidence: File timestamps in the mimo queue: 192 go1 09:49-11:16 (died on neterr 'socket connection was closed'), go2 started 12:00 (44 min idle), done 12:28, verified on the board 13:23 (55 min). 196 go1 10:11-11:06 (neterr), go2 11:59 (53 min idle), done 12:36, accepted 13:22 (46 min). 193 without an outage: 09:56 -> 10:47 -> verified 10:50. 6 .neterr files. Board: network drop 11:07-11:18 plus a database lock, TLS errors 12:55-13:11 on 203; 'rungo4 resumes' exists now.
findings.improvement: (a) A watchdog relaunches a dead agent on the same brief within 2 minutes, with the resume note filled in automatically. (b) A verify script runs as soon as a .done file appears. It runs shasum -c, lists files changed after the SEAL time (mtime plus err-log edit lines), re-reads each number in the RESULTS table from its JSON, and writes a short stub for the director. The director then only reads the stub and runs the held-out probe, which is the valuable human step.
findings.expected_gain: About 1-1.5 hours saved on every piece hit by an outage, and about 30-45 minutes on every piece that waits in the verify queue. Together with the shared diff tool this is the main path to roughly 2x throughput.
findings.risk: An automatic verify stub could be trusted too much. Keep the rule that the director signs every acceptance and runs the held-out probe. The stub only helps and never accepts anything.

findings.title: Many registered FAILs come from test design, not the feature; add a pre-seal case-file check
findings.problem: A large share of registered FAILs happened because the sealed tests themselves were wrong. Each one costs a full re-registration cycle (1-3 hours). Examples: case-file bugs or impossible setups (163, 167), a sealed expectation that demanded the old bug (139c P4-09), the mark naming the wrong base (170), an improvement nobody predicted (167c), soak flakes under load or a startup race (153, 158, 192's 2 lost teaches). FAIL should stay FAIL, but these are preventable before the seal.
findings.evidence: Board lines 50, 51, 78, 109, 123, 150, 155: 170 'mark named the wrong base; the speed-up itself works', 167c 'an unpredicted improvement', 167 'case-file bug', 163 '7 sealed noMerge cases had an impossible setup', 139c 'sealed expectation requires the old bug', 158 soak '10 wrong under load' (0 when the director re-ran it alone), 153 'soak x2' (0 diffs when re-run alone). 192 RESULTS: soak 'lost first teach (startup mailbox race, proven in daemon log)'. Re-registrations needed: 164b, 187b, 180b, 162b, 139e.
findings.improvement: Before sealing, the director (or the shared tool) runs a mechanical check. Every case's expected value must be reachable from its setup on the base agent. Every expected output must differ from the base's current output only where the piece intends a change. The base name in the marks must match the brief. Fix the soak race: wait for daemon readiness before the first teach, and run the soak only when the Mac load is below a threshold (record the load in the report). For the 'unpredicted improvement' case, allow predictions in the form 'moves only in direction X' (e.g. wrong->correct or abstain, never ->wrong), which stays falsifiable without listing exact ids.
findings.expected_gain: Fewer re-registration cycles. Judging from today's board, perhaps a quarter to a third of registered FAILs would not happen. This is an estimate from the board, not a measured rate.
findings.risk: Direction-only predictions are looser. Limit them to reply-text or abstain moves, and keep exact-id predictions for anything touching stored facts.

findings.title: Ledger predictions are mostly certain restatements; separate rule checks from real forecasts
findings.problem: Predictions are written after the full pilot on the final code, and the code is deterministic, so they mostly restate the pilot numbers. About a quarter are process rules (run under 1500 s, no post-seal edits) at 0.95. The ledger therefore records very few surprises and says little about how good the director's foresight is. It also costs agent time and 400 KB of append-only text.
findings.evidence: artifacts/fable-predictions-ledger.md lines 1700-2126: 253 prediction lines, 60 of them process-rule predictions (1500 s / post-seal / shasum); outcomes 179 TRUE vs 11 FALSE. P192.5/P192.6 and P138i.6/P138i.7 are rule checks. P138i.1 lists exact pilot counts (76/81/92/38; t1b 75/83), which were known before it was written.
findings.improvement: Keep the sealed pass marks, which carry the honesty. In the ledger, (a) turn the rule checks into a fixed checklist line in RESULTS instead of numbered predictions, and (b) ask for 1-2 genuine forecasts made at brief time by the director, before any pilot (e.g. 'bench moves <= 5', 'probe pass >= 80%'). Those forecasts are what show whether the director's model of the system is right.
findings.expected_gain: Small time saving per piece. The bigger gain is that the ledger starts measuring something useful (director calibration), which helps the expert/benchmark story.
findings.risk: Almost none, as long as registered bars and seals are unchanged.

keep_as_is: Sealing agent code, config and cases together with shasum before registered runs, plus the 09:56 rule that any post-seal change to them is a registered FAIL. It caught 180, 187, 164 and 167.
Registered FAIL stays FAIL, followed by one diagnosed follow-up with one change (e.g. 139d -> 139e, 162 -> 162b).
The director's held-out probe on every accepted piece with fresh fictional names. It keeps finding real gaps (e.g. 189b phrasings, 157c comma-less fillers).
Per-case comparison against the base agent (0 new wrong / wrong-write, moves only as predicted by id). This is the gate that actually matters.
Pilot-before-seal, and every case/seed reported as an integer count, never averaged.
Short final agent answers ('What it means' / 'What it does not mean') and plain-language board entries.
Disk guard and kill-by-exact-PID practice after the overnight incidents.
open_questions_for_ben: May the director re-baseline the frozen suites once (score stored facts, not reply wording) as its own sealed experiment, keeping the old suite outputs for history?
Is it OK to change the workflow so every new piece is built on the newest accepted base and landed right away, instead of collecting 9-11 pieces into big layer merges?
Is a direction-only prediction ('may move only toward correct or abstain') acceptable for reply-text changes, so an unexpected improvement no longer counts as a registered FAIL?

summary: The from-scratch talker exists, but it is not connected to the conversation loop. It is a 28.8M-parameter transformer with a copy head, pretrained on 617M tokens of SimpleStories: validation loss 1.56, BLiMP grammar test 67.4% against a 70% bar (FAIL). It was then fine-tuned to turn notebook records into sentences (talker120/120b/120d). After the plain-software brake it made 0 wrong statements in 500 test records, but its raw output was still unfaithful in 172/500 records (O6 FAIL, bar 50). Most remaining errors are cut-off names like 'Fara' for Farah. The current base agent loop138i still speaks through the hand-written template mouth (config 'mouth.stand_in: Loop138bMouth'), and the borrowed SmolLM mouth53 is not wired in either. So nothing trained by Ben produces the words a visitor sees. I ran a realistic uncle/dad conversation (43 turns) through loop138i. Teaching and asking in the robot possessive form works well, including 3-hop chains ("What is my sister's city's country?" -> "Your sister's city's country is Norwin."), plus corrections, forgetting, yes/no and 'What can you do?'. But about half of ordinary turns got the same long, clumsy three-sentence refusal, including 'Hello there.', 'Who are you?', 'Tell me about Mira.' and the natural two-hop 'What country does Mira live in?'. One turn made a wrong save ('Mira dog = called Pip'). A non-technical listener would conclude it barely understands English, even though the reasoning underneath is strong. Several fixes that passed on their own (156c small talk, 187b self questions, 188 statement fallback, 190 reverse questions, 192 correction wording) are not in 138i yet. They are waiting in the 138j merge, which is running now.

findings.title: Everyday two-hop questions fail even though the reasoner can answer them
findings.problem: The main advantage for the demo (joining two taught facts) only works when the question uses the stiff 'X's R's R' form. Natural wordings of the same question fall through to the refusal. This happens even when both facts are stored and the robot form of the same question works.
findings.evidence: Probe run2/run3 on loop138i. Taught 'My sister is Mira.' / 'Mira lives in Kestrel Bay.' / 'Kestrel Bay's country is Norwin.' (all 3 saved; events.jsonl raw: 'teach USER sister -> Mira', 'teach Mira city = Kestrel Bay', 'teach Kestrel Bay country = Norwin'). 'What is my sister's city's country?' -> 'Your sister's city's country is Norwin.' (correct). But 'Where does my sister live?', 'What country does Mira live in?', 'Which country does my sister live in?' and 'What country is Mira's city in?' all -> the generic decline. Also 'Kestrel Bay is in Norwin.' was not saved at all (run1). I found no board line that owns 'what country does X live in' or 'X is in Y' shapes.
findings.improvement: Add one ears piece that rewrites a small closed set of natural two-hop shapes into the possessive chain the composer already handles, then passes the result to the existing composer. Shapes: 'where does <chain> live' -> <chain>'s city; 'what/which country does <chain> live in' -> <chain>'s city's country; 'what country is <X> in' -> X's country. It should use the existing verb/city mapping. Add the teach shape '<Place> is in <Place>.' -> place's country, but only when the subject is already a stored city value, so ordinary sentences don't get misread. It never writes on an ask.
findings.expected_gain: The headline demo moment (teach two facts, ask one natural question, get the joined answer) works in plain English. That is the single turn most likely to impress the uncle/dad and the benchmark two-hop story.
findings.risk: False rewrites on look-alike sentences. Guard it the way 174/190 did: clarify-only, closed shapes, frozen-suite parity.

findings.title: The fallback reply is a three-sentence patchwork built to satisfy scorers, and it is what visitors see most
findings.problem: When the notebook misses and the router declines, the agent replies 'I do not know that from what you taught me. I have no record of it, so I will not guess. I didn't understand that, I don't know — could you say it another way?'. The code comment says this text was stitched together so that three different frozen judges (self scorer, bench scorer, redteam) each find their own marker phrase. The marks shaped the wording, not the listener. 188 fixes this only for statement-shaped turns; question turns keep the patchwork.
findings.evidence: scripts/fable_loop138_agent.py:82-93 (DECLINE_SUFFIX comment: 'the bare frozen HONEST_DECLINE is scored WRONG by the bench scorer... appends the redteam/bench abstain bits'). scripts/fable_loop188_agent.py:83-99 keeps QUESTION_FALLBACK188 = S105.HONEST_DECLINE + DECLINE_SUFFIX. Probes: this exact string was served on 26 of 43 probe turns, including 'Hello there.', 'How are you?', 'Who are you?', 'Tell me about yourself.', 'Can you talk?'.
findings.improvement: Use one short sentence with a helpful example, picked by the kind of turn. A question gets something like 'I don't know that — nobody has taught me. You can teach me, like "Kim's boss is Lee."'. Chat gets small talk. Update the frozen judges' abstain phrase lists once, in a sealed and disclosed judge change. Don't keep stacking phrases into the reply. The board already queues 'one fallback sentence'; this makes it a priority and says to change the judges.
findings.expected_gain: The most common reply stops sounding broken. A visitor hears one calm 'I don't know yet, teach me' line instead of a contradictory run-on ('I do not know... I didn't understand').
findings.risk: Changing a judge's phrase list must be its own sealed, disclosed change, or earlier registered results become hard to compare. Keep the old strings in the judge list too.

findings.title: Wrong save: 'Mira's dog is called Pip.' stores the value 'called Pip'
findings.problem: A very natural teaching sentence stores a garbage value. Later 'What is Mira's dog called?' answers 'I don't know Mira's dog called.' Related shapes also fail: "Mira's dog's name is Pip." -> decline, and 'What is the name of Mira's dog?' -> 'I don't know anyone called the name of Mira.'
findings.evidence: Probe run1 events.jsonl: '"raw": "teach Mira dog = called Pip"' (relation dog, non-functional); reply was 'Saved: Mira's dog is called Pip.', which hides the bad value. Run2: "Mira's dog's name is Pip." -> decline; "What is the name of Mira's dog?" -> "I don't know anyone called the name of Mira."
findings.improvement: One ears change: 'X's R is called/named V' and 'X's R's name is V' -> teach X R = V. Ask forms 'what is X's R called' and 'what is the name of X's R' -> ask X R. Add 'called/named' as a leading value word to the 167b/139b value screen, so it can never become the start of a stored value.
findings.expected_gain: Removes a real wrong write, which breaks the 0-wrong-writes promise, on a sentence people commonly use when teaching about pets and family.

findings.title: Answers sound robotic: no names in the chain, no 'because', 'city' instead of 'lives in'

The copy head then never has to spell 'Farah', which should remove most of the 149 truncation-related raw misses. (b) Wire Talker120dMouth into the loop behind a config flag ('voice: talker'), keeping the brake and the template fallback. Log raw-pass vs fallback counts per session, so Ben can see how much of the conversation his own model actually spoke.

findings.risk: Slot tokens change the training data format, so this needs a fresh registration. Needs a GPU slot (the fine-tune took seconds there) or a slow CPU fine-tune. CPU decode latency is about 0.27 s per sentence (20 decodes in 5.3 s in the smoke), which is fine. Whether this counts as Ben's own architecture is an open question.
